children: As India prepares to host the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12 and 13, the question of reducing dependence on the US dollar is set to remain one of the closely watched economic issues around the grouping. India is expected to discuss de-dollarisation with its BRICS partners, even as New Delhi has repeatedly maintained that it does not support creating a common BRICS currency or pursuing an agenda specifically aimed at replacing the dollar.

The issue has acquired greater significance because the three major BRICS economies at the centre of the debate, India, China and Russia, have taken distinctly different approaches to the use of national currencies and the dollar-based financial system.

At its simplest, de-dollarisation refers to reducing the use of the US dollar in international trade, payments and financial transactions. That can involve settling bilateral trade in national currencies, developing alternative payment systems or increasing the international use of currencies such as the rupee, Yuan or rouble.
For India, however, the approach has been more cautious.
India: Reduce dependence, but no common BRICS currency

New Delhi has supported greater use of national currencies for bilateral trade and has pushed for cheaper and more efficient cross-border payment mechanisms. But India has drawn a distinction between reducing transaction costs and pursuing an explicit anti-dollar agenda.
In August, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said India was not in favour of a separate BRICS currency.

“Bharat BRICS currency ke paksh mein nahin hai. Hum samarthan nai dete ki aisi koi BRICS currency jaisi nai yojna lai jaye. Bharat ka uske upar virodh hai (India is not in favour of a BRICS currency. We do not support the introduction of any such BRICS currency scheme; India opposes it),” Goyal said.
At the same time, India has been working on mechanisms that could reduce the need for dollar-based intermediaries in cross-border transactions.

Reuters reported in January that the Reserve Bank of India had proposed linking the official digital currencies of BRICS countries to facilitate cross-border trade and tourism payments. The proposal could reduce reliance on the dollar, although the RBI has maintained that efforts to internationalise the rupee are not aimed at promoting de-dollarisation.

RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in August that BRICS countries were discussing the possibility of linking their fast-payment systems and central bank digital currencies. He said the objective was to reduce the cost and improve the efficiency of cross-border payments.
India's position therefore centres on local-currency settlement, payment interoperability and reducing transaction costs, rather than replacing the dollar with a single BRICS currency.
China: Promote the yuan's international role
China's approach is more directly connected to increasing the global role of the Yuan.

The People's Bank of China said in August that it wanted to significantly expand the international use of the yuan in global trade and investment as part of its five-year plan. Reuters reported that the central bank also wants to maintain a stable exchange rate for the currency while expanding its international use.

Beijing has also been developing financial infrastructure and arrangements that allow more transactions to take place in Yuan. South China Morning Post reported in September that China and Egypt backed greater use of their respective currencies in trade and investment, while closer financial ties were being linked to Chinese investment in factories, energy projects and digital infrastructure.

China has also been encouraging the development of Yuan-denominated financial markets. In July, the country announced plans to waive certain fees for foreign issuers of panda bonds through 2028, a move aimed at supporting the yuan debt market and increasing the circulation of the currency outside China, according to South China Morning Post.

But China's approach does not mean an immediate abandonment of the dollar. The Yuan remains managed by the Chinese authorities, and Beijing has also been cautious about allowing sharp appreciation of the currency. Reuters reported in August that the People's Bank of China was resisting a rapid rise in the Yuan despite a weakening dollar.
China's strategy is therefore centred on expanding the yuan's international use and building payment and financial channels in which the dollar is not necessarily required.
Russia: Already operating heavily in national currencies

Russia's position is shaped by its experience with Western sanctions and restrictions on access to parts of the dollar-based financial system. However, Moscow has now sought to clarify that it does not formally advocate "de-dollarisation".

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on September 8 that Russia does not seek "de-dollarisation" and remains open to every acceptable method of payment. His comments came days before Russian President Vladimir Putin's expected participation in the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
“Some countries are using their national currency as a political tool,” Peskov said, without naming any country, according to Reuters.

At the same time, the practical shift away from the dollar is already substantial in Russia's trade relationships. Peskov said around 90% of transactions between Russia and BRICS countries are conducted in national currencies. He also said the issue of Russian companies accumulating excess Indian rupees because of bilateral trade was gradually being resolved.

Russia's approach is therefore less about announcing a formal campaign against the dollar and more about ensuring that its trade can continue through alternative payment arrangements and national currencies.
Why the US is watching closely

The United States is closely monitoring the BRICS debate because any significant expansion of non-dollar trade and payment systems could reduce the role of US financial infrastructure in international commerce.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned BRICS countries against efforts to replace the dollar. India itself has sought to avoid being seen as part of an explicit anti-dollar initiative.

The issue is particularly sensitive ahead of the New Delhi summit because BRICS is discussing practical mechanisms for increasing trade in national currencies. Business Standard reported that the September 12-13 summit agenda will include discussions on intra-BRICS financial mechanisms and ways to increase trade using national currencies. The report said Indian government sources indicated that New Delhi would be wary of any initiative that Washington could interpret as de-dollarisation.

The United States' concern also reflects the scale of the BRICS grouping. The bloc now includes 11 members, including major energy producers and large emerging economies. Greater use of local currencies in trade could, over time, create more payment channels operating outside the dollar-based financial system.

The issue is not simply about whether the dollar will be replaced. The current debate is also about whether countries can build a financial system in which the dollar is one of several major settlement options rather than the default currency for international trade.

That distinction is particularly important for India. New Delhi is seeking greater financial and payment autonomy while maintaining major economic ties with the United States. China is pushing to expand the international role of the yuan, while Russia has already shifted much of its BRICS trade towards national currencies.

Against that backdrop, the BRICS summit in New Delhi will offer a clearer indication of whether the grouping can move from discussions about alternative payment mechanisms to concrete arrangements, and how far India is prepared to go without endorsing an explicit campaign against the US dollar.

title: Is BRICS really trying to ditch the US dollar? What India, China and Russia really want and why US is watching closely
